messages.content: Write a recap post about what a team learned at an industry conference. Around 250 words.

**What we brought back from KubeCon**

Five of us went. We came home with roughly four hundred vendor stickers and one uncomfortable realization.

The realization: our incident review process is slower than almost every team we talked to. We'd assumed a 48-hour postmortem turnaround was tight. Two separate hallway conversations — one with a team at a payments company, one with a platform group at a retailer we won't name — put their number at same-day, with the write-up drafted while the incident channel is still open. Nobody treated that as heroic. It was just how they worked.

The talks were uneven, honestly. Much of the keynote material was vendors describing problems we don't have. But Priya's session pick on Wednesday paid for the trip by itself: a walkthrough of how one team cut build times by deleting tests instead of adding parallelism. They killed 300 tests that had never once caught a real bug. Build went from 22 minutes to 9.

Sana spent most of Thursday in the eBPF track and has opinions now. Ask her.

What changes for us: we're moving postmortem drafting into the incident itself, starting with the next Sev-2. Marcus is auditing our suite for the never-failed-once category. And we're sending three people next year instead of five — the value was in the conversations between sessions, and five of us clustered together mostly talked to each other.

Slides and notes are in the shared drive.

**Notes from KubeCon**

Five of us flew out. We came back with a sack of vendor stickers nobody wants and one thing we'd rather not have learned.

That thing: our incident review is slower than nearly every team we spoke to. We'd thought a 48-hour postmortem turnaround was aggressive. Two separate hallway conversations, one with a payments team and one with a platform group at a retailer we'll leave unnamed, put them both at same-day, with the draft written while the incident channel is still open. Neither treated it as remarkable. It was just Tuesday.

The talks were a mixed bag. Keynotes were largely vendors describing problems we don't have. But Priya's Wednesday pick covered the cost of the trip on its own: a team that cut build times by deleting tests instead of parallelizing them. Three hundred tests that had never once caught a real bug, gone. Twenty-two minutes down to nine.

Sana spent Thursday in the eBPF track and now has opinions. Go ask her.

What changes: postmortem drafting moves inside the incident, starting with the next Sev-2. Marcus is auditing the suite for anything in the never-failed-once bucket. And three of us go next year instead of five — the value was in the conversations between sessions, and five people traveling together mostly ended up talking to each other.

Slides and notes are in the shared drive.
